title: Exercise vs. Antidepressants: What the Research Actually Shows
description: Does exercise really work as well as medication for depression? A deep dive into the research, what it means, and practical recommendations.

content.text: Headlines claim exercise works as well as antidepressants. Is it true? The answer is nuanced—and important.
A 2023 meta-analysis of 218 studies found exercise significantly reduced depression, with effects comparable to psychotherapy and antidepressants for mild-moderate depression.
content.citation: Singh et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2023

content.text: The landmark SMILE trial found exercise and sertraline equally effective at 4 months, with exercise showing lower relapse rates at 10-month follow-up.
content.citation: Blumenthal et al., Archives of Internal Medicine, 1999

content.text: Exercise appears comparably effective to antidepressants and therapy. The effect sizes are similar across treatments.
Less clear. Most exercise studies exclude severe cases. Starting exercise when you can barely get out of bed is incredibly difficult without additional support.

items: Aerobic exercise (running, cycling) has the most evidence
Yoga shows promise, especially for anxiety
Walking is effective (low barrier to entry)
Any movement is better than none

content.text: Most studies showing benefits used: 30-60 minutes per session, 3-5 times per week, at moderate intensity. But benefits appear at lower doses too.
The hardest part of using exercise for depression is that depression makes it incredibly hard to exercise. This is where medication or therapy can help create enough energy to get started.

items: Pair with something rewarding (podcast, coffee after)
Consider exercise as complement to other treatment, not replacement
Any movement counts—perfection is the enemy

content.text: Exercise is a legitimate depression treatment with evidence comparable to medication—for mild-moderate cases. It's not a replacement for professional treatment, especially for severe depression. The best approach? Combine exercise with whatever else helps you: therapy, medication, social support. They work together.
